questions.stem: What is a quadrat?

options.text: A square frame placed on the ground to record the organisms within it
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nets trap animals; quadrats frame an area for counting.
Soil slides are a different tool.
Tape measures length; a quadrat frames area.

questions.stem: Which record suits grass or moss, where counting individuals is impractical?

options.explanation: Weight is not the standard abundance measure here.

options.text: Percentage cover, estimating the quadrat area the species occupies
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Counting is impractical for grass, hence cover estimates.
Root depth is not a quadrat record.

questions.stem: Which abundance record counts different species rather than individuals?

options.explanation: Cover tracks area, not species counts.
Weight measures none of these.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That counts one species, not richness.

questions.stem: Why are plants the usual subjects of quadrat studies?

options.text: Because animals refuse to enter frames
options.explanation: Animals move through quadrats; plants simply stay put.
Plants are often abundant; stillness is the point.
Quadrats work on land and in water.

options.text: Because plants stay still, so the frame records their abundance reliably
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A student must compare plant abundance in two fields. Which tool set fits?

options.text: Quadrats with a random number generator and tape measures
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Those measure weather, not abundance.
Pitfall traps sample moving animals, not framed plant counts.

options.text: A quadrat with no placement plan
options.explanation: Random placement is required for fair sampling.

questions.stem: State what a quadrat is used for.
questions.modelAnswer: A quadrat frames an area of ground so the organisms inside can be recorded to estimate population size or abundance.

questions.stem: Name the abundance method used when it is hard to count individual plants.
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage cover estimates the share of the quadrat area occupied by a species when counting individuals is impractical.

questions.stem: Explain why quadrat sizes are quoted in square metres.
questions.modelAnswer: Quadrat sizes are quoted in square metres because the frame encloses an area, and abundance is compared per unit area, not per length.

questions.stem: A moss patch spreads unevenly across a quadrat. Which record fits best?
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage cover fits best, since moss individuals are hard to separate, so the student estimates the fraction of quadrat area the moss occupies.

questions.stem: Why must quadrat placement be random?

options.explanation: Plant growth is unaffected; sampling bias is the issue.

options.text: Random placement makes the sample representative of the survey area
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The point is fair sampling, not fun.
Randomness protects the data, not the frame.

questions.stem: Which item converts coordinates into a position on the ground?

options.explanation: It makes numbers; the tapes map them to ground.
A pencil records results, not positions.

options.text: The two tape measures laid out as axes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The key identifies species, it does not position frames.

questions.stem: What does a species key add to the investigation?

options.explanation: The generator handles coordinates.
The key identifies, it does not frame.
Weather is not part of the key.

options.text: Reliable identification of the species found in each quadrat
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Coordinates 4,5 are drawn for a 10 by 10 metre area. Where does the quadrat land?

options.text: Four metres along one axis and five metres along the other
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: At the centre of the area
options.explanation: The centre would be 5,5, not 4,5.

options.text: Four steps from any edge chosen freely
options.explanation: The axes fix the position precisely.
Preference defeats random sampling.

questions.stem: Which apparatus item guards against missing species you cannot name?

options.explanation: It picks coordinates, not names.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Tapes frame the area; keys name the species.
The frame samples; identification needs the key.

questions.stem: List the apparatus for a two-area quadrat comparison.
questions.modelAnswer: Two tape measures, a quadrat, a random number generator and a species key make up the apparatus list.

questions.stem: State how the first quadrat position is chosen.
questions.modelAnswer: A random number generator produces coordinates, and the quadrat is placed at that point within the laid-out survey area.

questions.stem: Explain why bias enters when students pick quadrat spots by eye.
questions.modelAnswer: Choosing spots by eye biases the sample towards whatever looks interesting, so random coordinates keep the estimate honest for the whole survey area.

questions.stem: A student drops every quadrat on the path edge. Judge the sample.
questions.modelAnswer: The sample is biased, since path edges differ from the rest of the area, so the population estimate will not represent the survey area fairly.

questions.stem: Why average the quadrat counts before comparing areas?

options.explanation: The method is statistical, not cosmetic.
Averaging enables comparison; it does not force equality.

options.text: Averaging smooths quadrat-to-quadrat variation into one fair estimate
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because single counts are always wrong
options.explanation: Single counts are valid data; averaging reduces variability.

questions.stem: A quadrat count misses seedlings hidden by bracken. Which limitation is this?

options.explanation: The frame is fine; the counting technique slipped.
Weather is not the named limitation.
Identification is not the issue; visibility is.

options.text: Easy-to-miss individuals hidden by another species
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which fix suits seedlings hidden under leaves in a quadrat?

options.text: Lift leaves gently with a pencil or stick to check underneath
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Speed worsens misses; checking underneath fixes them.
Skipping loses data instead of revealing it.
Guessing defeats the estimate.

questions.stem: Which abiotic factor list fits a plant abundance comparison?

options.explanation: Frame colour changes nothing ecological.

options.text: Light, minerals, water, pH, temperature and salinity
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Those are biotic factors, not abiotic.
The key is apparatus, not an environmental factor.

questions.stem: Area A holds double the abundance of area B. What explains it?

options.explanation: Assuming error without cause is weak; factors explain it.
Plants stay put; conditions differ instead.

options.text: Differences in biotic pressures or abiotic conditions between the areas
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Quadrats standardise area, so size cancels out.

questions.stem: State one biotic factor that influences plant abundance between two areas.
questions.modelAnswer: Competition is a biotic factor that influences the abundance recorded in each survey area.

questions.stem: State one limitation of counting organisms in a quadrat and its solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Individuals are easily missed under other species, so a pencil or stick lifts the leaves to check underneath.

questions.stem: Explain why both biotic and abiotic factors must be considered when comparing areas.
questions.modelAnswer: Both must be considered because abundance responds to living pressures such as competition and to non-living conditions such as light and water, so either could explain a difference.

questions.stem: A shady area yields half the count of a sunny one. Explain using factors.
questions.modelAnswer: Light intensity differs between the areas, so photosynthesis and growth differ, making the abiotic difference the likely driver of the lower abundance.
